summary: Describes registries for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol, covering Mode bit positions and Control Command numbers, which IANA has established. It updates RFC 4656.

plainLanguage.summary: A list is kept so that everyone agrees on what each setting number means.

questions: what is the owamp control command number registry
subtitle: The IANA registries that track new Mode bits and Control Command numbers for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol.

tldr.problem: OWAMP had no registries for future extensions, even though a first new feature was being proposed and TWAMP already had a registry of its own.
tldr.mechanism: The memo asks IANA to create an OWAMP-Control Command Number registry and an OWAMP-Modes registry, gives each its initial contents, and requires IETF Review for changes.
tldr.outcome: New OWAMP features now have defined places to be assigned. The Modes registry already lists bit position 4 for the IKEv2-derived shared secret key extension of RFC 7717.

today: RFC 7718 is a Proposed Standard from December 2015 that updates RFC 4656. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OWAMP Needed Registries
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656) was prepared to support measurements of metrics from the IETF IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group. The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) extends it. TWAMP drew wide review, which produced recommendations for new features, so a registry of features was set up for TWAMP.

No new features had been proposed for OWAMP until RFC 7717. This memo therefore establishes the needed OWAMP registries and updates RFC 4656.
sections.plainLanguage: The twin protocol already had a list of approved add-ons, but OWAMP did not. When someone finally wanted to add something, a list was needed.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content: The memo describes and requests registries for future OWAMP extensions and supplies their initial contents. IANA already administers the TWAMP Parameters registry, and this request follows a similar form, with one exception that the text points out in the Modes registry: OWAMP-Modes entries are assigned by bit position and carry no separate value.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sets up the lists and fills in the first lines, copying how the twin protocol's list was done.

sections.title: How the Registries Are Managed
sections.content:
Both registries are small. The Command Number registry has a maximum of 256 values, and the Modes registry rests on only 32 bit positions, each conveying one feature. Because of this, and because OWAMP is an IETF protocol, both MUST be updated only by IETF Review as defined in RFC 5226: an RFC that documents the registry use and is approved by the IESG.

For the Modes registry, IANA SHOULD allocate monotonically increasing bit positions when requested.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only a few slots on each list, so a change needs a formal, approved document, and new bits are handed out in order.

sections.title: The Control Command Number Registry
sections.content:
OWAMP-Control Command Numbers are carried in the first octet of OWAMP-Control-Client command messages, as in Section 3 of RFC 4656. The initial contents are: 0 Reserved, 1 Request-Session, 2 Start-Sessions, 3 Stop-Sessions, 4 Fetch-Sessions, 5 to 253 Unassigned, 254 Experimentation, and 255 Reserved.

Value 254 is the one experimental value currently assigned in this registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of request has a number. Some are used, a big block is empty, and one number is kept for people to try out ideas.

sections.title: The OWAMP-Modes Registry
sections.content:
Modes appear in the Server Greeting and Set-up Response messages (Section 3.1 of RFC 4656). They are currently single bits in a 32-bit Modes field, though a more complex encoding may be used in future. The initial contents are bit 0 Unauthenticated, bit 1 Authenticated, bit 2 Encrypted, bit 3 Reserved, bit 4 IKEv2-derived Shared Secret Key (from RFC 7717), and bits 5 to 31 Unassigned. No experimental bit positions are assigned.

The Server sends the bit-wise OR of the modes it is willing to support. With no other features active, the 27 most significant bits MUST be zero. A client conforming to RFC 4656 MAY ignore the 29 most significant bits or MAY support features signalled there.

OWAMP and TWAMP mode registries may grow apart, so no effort is made to coordinate them except for Reserved bit 3, which stays available for a mixed security mode like the one in RFC 5618.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of 32 light switches, one per feature. The server flips on the switches for what it can do, and old clients just ignore switches they do not know.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Because the memo only documents the creation of registries, it raises no new security or privacy issues. The considerations for active measurement of live networks in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357 still apply, and privacy considerations for measurement systems are in RFC 7594.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a list does not open any new doors, so there is nothing new to guard. The old safety rules still count.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Kept for a possible mixed security mode.
